## ARGUMENT

### A debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibits a debt collector from using "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. That prohibition reaches, among other things, "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." *Id.* § 1692e(10). Congress enacted the statute to protect consumers from abusive collection practices, and this Court construes it liberally to serve that remedial purpose. *See Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006); *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008).

**1. The least sophisticated debtor standard governs.**

This Court evaluates collection communications from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000); *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298 (3d Cir. 2008). The standard is objective and is lower than that of a reasonable debtor. It protects the gullible and the shrewd alike. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454; *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221. It also preserves a check against liability for bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations. The least sophisticated debtor is presumed to possess a basic level of understanding and a willingness to read the collection notice with some care. *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221; *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011).

**2. A letter is deceptive if it is reasonably susceptible to an inaccurate reading.**

Applying that standard, this Court has held that a collection letter is deceptive when it can reasonably be read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455; *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 222; *Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 149 (3d Cir. 2013); *Tatis v. Allied Interstate, LLC*, 882 F.3d 422, 427 (3d Cir. 2018). The inquiry does not ask which reading the collector intended, or even which reading is most natural. Nor must the consumer show that the collector acted knowingly or willfully. If one reasonable reading is false or misleading, the collector bears the consequence of its own ambiguity. A collector controls the language of its letters, and the burden of clarity belongs on the party that drafts the communication, not on the consumer who must decide how to respond to it. *See Caprio*, 709 F.3d at 149–51; *Tatis*, 882 F.3d at 427–30.

The standard asks only whether an inaccurate reading is reasonable. It does not matter that an accurate reading is also available, because a letter that permits both readings still deceives the debtor who adopts the wrong one. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455. In *Wilson* and *Brown*, this Court looked past the letters' literal accuracy and asked how an unsophisticated consumer could understand them. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 355–56; *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454–55.

**3. The inaccurate reading need only be material.**

A statement violates § 1692e only if it is material, meaning it is capable of influencing the debtor's decision or ability to pay or challenge the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 421 (3d Cir. 2015). The materiality requirement screens out technical falsehoods that could not affect a consumer's handling of the debt. It does not require proof that any particular consumer was actually misled. *See id.* at 419–21.

**4. Application.**

Defendant's letter fails this test. [Quote or describe the challenged language.] One reasonable reading, and the one Defendant presumably intends, is that [accurate meaning]. But the least sophisticated debtor could just as reasonably read the same language to mean that [inaccurate meaning]. That reading is false because [explain]. It is also material. A debtor who adopted it might [pay a debt not owed, pay an inflated amount, forgo a dispute, or otherwise change her response to the letter]. That is the kind of influence on a consumer's decision that *Jensen* identifies. 791 F.3d at 421.

Because the letter can reasonably be read in two ways, one of them inaccurate and material, it violates § 1692e. This Court should reverse the district court's contrary judgment and hold that Defendant's letter is deceptive as a matter of law.
